d1.mp3: In 1994, Roger Bueller and two colleagues asked a room of students one question about their own final paper. How many days until it is finished? Not a deadline, their own honest estimate. The average came back at 33.9 days. Then the researchers waited. The papers came in at 55.5 days and fewer than three students in 10 finished inside the time they had given themselves. Nobody lied and nobody was lazy. They were describing a future that did not arrive.
d2.mp3: I did not decide not to do it. That is the part people get wrong about this. I sat down, I opened the folder, and something in me said, Not now, later tonight. And the relief was immediate. That is the honest bit, and it is the bit nobody admits. The moment I closed it I felt fine. Then Thursday morning arrived and the same folder was there with less time around it and the same feeling waiting inside it. I had not saved anything. I had only moved it.
d3.mp3: There is one thing in this research that changes the numbers, and it is much smaller than people expect. It is not motivation, and it is not discipline. It is writing down when and where. A person who says, I will work on this at some point this week, does roughly what you would guess. A person who says, Thursday, 9 in the morning, at the kitchen table, does substantially more of it. Same person, same task, same week. The only difference is that the plan named a moment and a place, so the moment can arrive.
